newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya Airways profits fall after privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Kenya Airways profits fall after privatisation.

text.p: Kenya Airways, hit by rising fuel and labour costs, posted a 6.9 percent fall in first-half net profits on Thursday and said it was facing tough times after privatisation this year.
Net profits before tax and foreign exchange were 638 million shillings ($11.44 million) in the six months to September 30 compared to 685 million shillings in the same period last year.

"Forecasts for the remainder of the year to March 31, 1997 include cost savings and revenue improvements as previously announced. But profits are expected to fall below last year's results," Kenya Airways said in a statement.
In the year ended March 1996 the company made a net profit before tax and exceptional items of 1.99 billion shillings, compared with 885.60 million the year before.
"Industry analysts expect oil prices to remain at present levels for the time being and this will continue to depress operating profits," it added.
Public relations manager Koome Mwambia told Reuters: "We are facing some hard times. But I think we should be able to pull through. Half the year is not the full year."
John Munge, managing director of leading brokerage house Shah, Munge & Partners added: "The results are actually good for an airline, taking in market conditions at the time."
Kenya completed privatisation of the airline this year, with Royal Dutch Airlines KLM NV buying 26 percent and another 51 percent floated on the Nairobi Stock Exchange.
The sale of 235 million shares by the Kenyan government, which retained 23 percent, was the biggest privatisation so far on the Nairobi Stock Exchange.
The shares were floated at 11.25 shillings, rose initially to 15 shillings but closed at 8.95 shillings on Wednesday.
The airline said it would pay an interim dividend of 25 Kenyan cents for shareholders on the register on December 31. Last year, while still state-owned, it paid no dividends.

At the annual meeting last week shareholders said they were unhappy about the poor share price performance, the airline's attempt to retain government-appointed directors and its inability to make any strategic decisions without the prior approval of KLM.

They also complained about the handling of a major dispute involving pilots. Earlier this year, a court awarded pilots nearly $7 million in salary arrears -- saying they were some of the poorest paid professionals in the business.
"This award could not have been predicted by management," public relations manager Mwambia said.
"On the role of KLM, in the long-term it is only KLM that may help us lift from our current turbulence. We can only gain from this partnership."

A special meeting on December 5 will decide the question of directors. When Kenya Airways was government-owned, the state appointed nine directors. But shareholders say it should relinquish that right.
